During the decade of the sixties, U.S. population increased 13.3 percent. Almost 85 percent of the population increase occurred in 243 SMSA's.* Within the SMSA's, about 80 percent of the increases took place outside the central cities. 7/ In 1970, U.S. population was about 2.7 times what it had been in 1900. For suburban areas, it was about six times what it was in 1900. The differential between central cities and suburbs in rate of population growth has widened since 1940. During the 1960's, central cities as a group increased by 6.4 percent. The rate of growth for sections outside central cities within SMSA's was 26.7 percent. As a result, those central cities as a group now have fewer inhabitants than their surrounding suburban areas. 8/
The information presented above relative to the direction of population growth and employment is further enhanced by the Arthur D. Little report dated October 10, 1975. 9/ This report was prepared for the Freight Forwarders Institute and is a representation to this proceeding. Further reference will be made to that report in regard to proposals for a population-mileage formula.
*
Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas.
